headline: Easy-run cardiac drift has dropped meaningfully over the past month, pointing to genuine aerobic adaptation beneath a near-flat volume trend.
confidence_reasons: Multiple data sources active in last 3 days
summary:
The volume numbers look almost identical across the two blocks, but the more interesting signal is what's happening inside those runs: your easy-run heart rate has fallen noticeably at comparable efforts, which is a cleaner marker of aerobic development than distance alone. That kind of shift doesn't happen by accident — it reflects accumulated adaptation from consistent work, including the June 27th threshold effort and the 44 km long run earlier in the month.

The 20-week streak is worth acknowledging not as a streak for its own sake, but because it represents a level of structural consistency that underpins adaptation. Volume can fluctuate; showing up doesn't. Strength frequency has dipped slightly this block, which is worth keeping an eye on but doesn't yet represent a meaningful trend — five sessions in four weeks is still a functional load for a hybrid athlete maintaining capacity rather than peaking.
watch_items: Watch whether the easy-run HR decline continues or plateaus — further drops would confirm ongoing aerobic adaptation, a stall would suggest the current stimulus needs adjusting
Monitor whether strength frequency stabilises back toward the prior rhythm or continues to soften — one block is noise, two in a row starts to matter
After back-to-back easy days following the June 27th threshold session, observe how your legs feel on the next quality or long effort — useful signal for recovery rate at current load
The lactate threshold data point is brand new — worth watching whether repeat testing over coming weeks shows consistency or reveals the June 27th effort as an outlier

evidence_items.text: ▼ Easy-run HR averaging 147 bpm vs 157 bpm prior period (comparable-effort runs, 6 vs 6 runs)
▲ 4-week volume 127 km vs 125 km prior block (+2%)
